usage: to talk, to have a conversation
the default verb; 이야기 itself is a noun, so you almost always pair it with 하다
나누다 (to share/divide) is warmer and more two-sided than 하다 — used for heartfelt talks
always 듣다 (hear/listen), never 보다; you 'hear' a story even when reading is involved
the adjective 재미있는 sits before the noun; 이야기가 재미있다 puts it after
examples: 친구하고 이야기해요.
I talk with my friend.
하고 = 'with' in casual speech; here 이야기하다 works as one verb, no 를 needed
어제 선생님하고 진로 이야기를 나눴어요.
Yesterday I had a talk with my teacher about my career path.
나누다 signals a meaningful, mutual conversation, not idle chatter
할머니가 옛날이야기를 들려주셨어요.
Grandma told me an old folktale.
옛날이야기 = a folk/old-times tale; 들려주다 = to tell (lit. let one hear), with 셨 honoring grandma
nuance: 이야기 covers both a 'story' (a tale, an account) and 'talking/chatting' in the abstract, so 이야기하다 is the everyday verb for 'to talk, to converse.' The nearest neighbor is 대화(對話): 대화 is a slightly more formal, two-directional 'dialogue/conversation,' while 이야기 is the warm, native-Korean word for casual talk and also for a narrated story — a meaning 대화 never has. Note 말하다 means 'to say/speak (utter words)' and centers on the act of producing speech, whereas 이야기하다 frames a whole exchange or telling. In real speech Koreans constantly contract 이야기 to 얘기, so 얘기해요 and 이야기해요 are identical. The English-speaker pitfall: 'story' makes learners reach for 보다 ('I saw a story'), but a story is something you 듣다 (hear) or 읽다 (read), and 'talk to someone' is 누구하고 이야기하다 with 하고/랑, not the English 'talk to' mapped onto an object particle.

usage: the classic collocation; its opposite is 나쁜 소식 or the heavier 슬픈 소식 (sad news)
news 'arrives at your ear,' so 듣다, not 보다 — even for written word
전하다 (to convey) is the verb for relaying news to a third person
to lose touch (lit. news is cut off)
끊기다 = to be severed; describes losing all contact with someone
examples: 좋은 소식이 있어요.
I have good news.
있다 marks existence; 소식이 있다 = 'there is news / I have news'
오랜만에 옛 친구 소식을 들었어요.
I heard word about an old friend for the first time in ages.
소식 here means 'how they're doing,' not a headline; 오랜만에 = after a long time
이사 간 뒤로 그 사람 소식이 끊겼어요.
I've lost touch with that person since they moved away.
소식이 끊기다 is the natural way to say 'we lost contact'
nuance: 소식(消息) is Sino-Korean — 消 'disappear/wane' + 息 'breath/rest' — and originally meant the ebb and flow of things; today it means 'news, word, tidings,' especially personal news about how a person or situation is faring. The sharp contrast is with 뉴스: 뉴스 is the English loanword reserved for broadcast/press news (TV, newspapers, current events), whereas 소식 is the news of individuals and private matters — a friend's wedding, a relative's health. Compare also 정보(情報) 'information/data,' which is impersonal facts you look up. Natural partners are 좋은/나쁜 소식, 소식을 전하다/듣다, and the poignant 소식이 없다/끊기다 ('haven't heard from them'). The pitfall for English speakers: 'I watched the news' tempts 소식을 봤어요, but media news is 뉴스를 봤어요; reserve 소식 for word about people, and remember you 듣다 (hear) personal news rather than 보다 it.

usage: 거짓말 is a noun, so 'to lie' = 거짓말하다 / 거짓말을 하다, never bare 거짓말
set idiom; 새빨간 'crimson' intensifies it to 'total, blatant lie'
-쟁이 turns it into a (mildly mocking) person-noun, like 'fibber'
as if by magic (lit. like a lie)
거짓말 + 처럼; describes something so good/sudden it seems unreal
examples: 거짓말하지 마세요.
Please don't lie.
-지 마세요 = 'please don't'; here 거짓말하다 acts as one verb
동생이 또 새빨간 거짓말을 했어요.
My little sibling told another barefaced lie.
새빨간 거짓말 = a flat-out lie; 또 = 'again,' hinting it's a habit
거짓말! 진짜 합격했어?
No way! You really passed?
among friends 거짓말! is an exclamation of happy disbelief, not an accusation
nuance: 거짓말 is built transparently from native roots: 거짓 'false, untrue' + 말 'words/speech,' literally 'false words,' i.e. a lie. As a noun it needs 하다 to become the verb 거짓말하다 ('to lie'). The near-synonym to separate it from is 변명(辨明) 'excuse/justification': a 거짓말 is a deliberate falsehood, while a 변명 is a (possibly true) defense or rationalization for one's behavior. Note also 농담 'joke' is harmless fun, not deception. Collocations to know: 새빨간 거짓말 'barefaced lie,' 거짓말을 들키다 'get caught lying,' 거짓말쟁이 'liar.' A lovely register twist: among close friends, 거짓말! shouted alone means 'No way! / You're kidding!' as delighted shock. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'lie' is itself a verb, so learners say 거짓말 alone to mean 'lie' — but you must say 거짓말을 하다; and don't confuse the noun with 진짜 'real' or 사실(事實) 'fact, truth,' its true opposite.

usage: to make a joke, to kid
농담 is a noun; 'to joke' = 농담하다 / 농담을 하다
set phrase to defuse a remark and show you didn't mean it
-(으)로 marks manner: 'in a joking way,' often 농담으로 한 말 'something said in jest'
fixed idiom for a remark that's partly a real hint
examples: 농담이에요, 화내지 마세요.
I'm joking, don't be upset.
tacking on 농담이에요 instantly softens what you just said
그 사람은 농담을 진담으로 받아들였어요.
He took the joke as if I meant it seriously.
진담 = serious talk; the pair 농담 vs 진담 is the key contrast
농담 반 진담 반으로 같이 가자고 했어요.
Half joking, half serious, I suggested we go together.
농담 반 진담 반 hints the speaker partly means it
nuance: 농담(弄談) is Sino-Korean — 弄 'to play with, tease' + 談 'talk' — literally 'playful talk,' i.e. a joke meant to amuse, not to wound. Its built-in opposite is 진담(眞談) 'earnest/serious talk' (眞 'true' + 談 'talk'), and Koreans lean on the pair constantly: 농담이야, 진담이야? 'Are you kidding or serious?' Distinguish it from 거짓말 'a lie': a 농담 is openly non-serious fun that listeners are meant to recognize, while a 거짓말 is meant to deceive. Also separate it from 장난 'a prank/mischief (often an action),' versus 농담 which is verbal wit. Natural collocations: 농담을 하다, 농담으로 한 말, 농담이 심하다 'the joke goes too far,' 농담 반 진담 반. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 농담 as a verb on its own — say 농담하다; and 'You're joking!' as an exclamation is usually 거짓말! or 진짜?, not 농담!, since 농담이에요 is what YOU say about YOUR OWN remark to signal you weren't serious.

usage: to contact, to get in touch
연락 is a noun; 'to contact' = 연락하다 / 연락을 하다
to hear from someone (lit. contact comes)
오다, not 을 오다 — the contact is the subject that 'comes to' you: 연락이 오다
되다 here = 'manages to connect'; 연락이 안 돼요 = 'I can't reach them'
연락 + 처(處) 'place/point' → the point at which to reach you = phone/contact info
examples: 나중에 연락할게요.
I'll get in touch later.
-ㄹ게요 = a casual promise about your own action
친구한테서 연락이 왔어요.
I heard from my friend.
한테서 = 'from (a person)'; 연락이 오다 takes 이/가, not 을/를
전화도 문자도 연락이 안 돼요.
I can't reach them by call or text.
연락이 되다/안 되다 = to (not) get through; note 도…도 'neither…nor'
nuance: 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean — 連 'connect/link' + 絡 'tie, network' — literally 'to link up,' and it covers ANY channel of reaching a person: a call, a text, a message, an email. The near-synonym to contrast is 소식: 연락 is the ACT/CHANNEL of getting in touch ('drop me a line'), while 소식 is the CONTENT/word about how someone is. Compare 통화(通話) 'a phone call (specifically)' — narrower than 연락. The crucial grammar quirk for English speakers: 연락 flips between particles. When YOU reach out it's 연락을 하다 / 연락하다 (object 를), but when contact COMES to you it's 연락이 오다 and reachability is 연락이 되다 (subject 이/가) — saying 연락을 오다 is a classic error. Also, English 'contact someone' has a direct object, so learners drop the person-marking 한테/에게: it should be 친구한테 연락하다, and incoming contact is 친구한테서/에게서 연락이 오다. 연락처 (with 처) means your number/details, not the verb.

Dropping the person particle: 'contact me' is 저한테 연락하세요, not 저를 연락하세요.
Confusing 연락 (the act of getting in touch) with 소식 (the news/word itself) — 연락이 없다 = 'they haven't reached out'; 소식이 없다 = 'no word on how they are.'

usage: 부탁 is a noun; 'to make a request' = 부탁하다 / 부탁을 하다
I have a favor to ask
softly opens a request; 있다 marks 'there is a favor (on my side)'
I look forward to working with you (lit. I kindly entrust this)
humble 드리다 form; the standard polite phrase at introductions/handovers
들어주다 = to grant/heed a request; 좀 softens it
examples: 부탁이 하나 있어요.
I have one favor to ask.
하나 'one' makes the ask feel small and polite
이것 좀 부탁해요.
Could you take care of this for me?
좀 softens; 부탁해요 here = 'I'm entrusting this to you'
앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
I look forward to working with you from now on.
the go-to humble greeting when joining a team or starting a project
nuance: 부탁(付託) is Sino-Korean — 付 'hand over/entrust' + 託 'commit, consign' — literally 'to entrust (a matter) to someone,' i.e. to ask a favor. The near-synonym to separate is 요청(要請) 'a (formal) request/demand': 요청 is businesslike and official (a 요청서 is a request form, 협조를 요청하다 'request cooperation'), whereas 부탁 is personal and softens the asker into the lower, indebted position. Compare 부탁 with 명령 'an order/command,' its opposite in power. Register is the heart of this word: among equals 부탁해요, but upward or formally you switch to the humble verb 드리다 → 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드립니다, a set phrase at introductions, handovers, and emails meaning roughly 'please look kindly on me/this.' Collocations: 부탁을 들어주다 'grant a favor,' 부탁을 거절하다 'refuse,' 어려운 부탁. The English-speaker pitfall: 'ask someone a favor' makes learners say 누구를 부탁하다, but the person takes 한테/에게 (친구한테 부탁하다), and bare 부탁 can't be the verb — you need 부탁하다 or the humble 부탁드리다 in polite settings.

usage: always 쓰다 (write), never 만들다 (make); you 'write,' not 'make,' a letter
보내다 = to send; its pair is 받다 'to receive'
부치다 specifically = drop in the mail; narrower than 보내다
손 'hand' + 편지; carries a warm, heartfelt nuance vs typed mail
examples: 엄마한테 편지를 써요.
I write a letter to my mom.
한테 = 'to (a person)'; the recipient takes 한테/에게
친구한테서 손편지를 받았어요.
I received a handwritten letter from my friend.
한테서 = 'from'; 손편지 stresses it was warmly handwritten
우체국에서 편지를 부쳤어요.
I mailed the letter at the post office.
부치다 (post) is more precise than 보내다 for physical mail
nuance: 편지(便紙/片紙) is Sino-Korean — commonly written 便紙, with 紙 'paper' — denoting a paper letter you write by hand and send by post. The contrast to draw is with newer media words: 이메일 (email), 문자 (a text message), 메시지/카톡 (an instant message). 편지 specifically evokes paper and ink, so a 손편지 (handwritten letter) feels especially sincere and personal in Korean culture. Note the verbs differ from English instincts: you 쓰다 (write) a letter, 보내다/부치다 (send/post) it, and 받다 (receive) it — and 부치다 is the precise 'put in the mail.' Collocations: 편지를 쓰다/보내다/받다, 답장 'a reply.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'make a card/letter' tempts 편지를 만들다, but a letter is written (쓰다), not made; and don't let 편지 blur into 편의점 (convenience store) — they merely look alike. Recipients are marked with 한테/에게 (또는 honorific 께), senders with 한테서/에게서.

Mis-marking people: write 'to' someone with 한테/에게/께 (엄마한테 편지를 쓰다), and 'from' with 한테서/에게서.

usage: 답장 is a noun; 'to reply (in writing)' = 답장하다 / 답장을 하다
보내다 = to send; you send a written 답장 back
the standard way to say someone hasn't written back
기다리다 = to wait; common at the end of emails/letters
examples: 문자에 답장했어요.
I replied to the text.
에 marks the message you reply 'to'; 답장하다 acts as one verb
빨리 답장을 보내 주세요.
Please send a reply soon.
-아/어 주세요 = 'please do (for me)'; 빨리 = quickly
이메일을 보냈는데 아직 답장이 없어요.
I sent an email but there's still no reply.
답장이 없다 = haven't heard back; 아직 = 'still, yet'
nuance: 답장(答狀) is Sino-Korean — 答 'to answer' + 狀 'a written document/letter' — literally 'an answering document,' i.e. a written reply to a letter, text, or email. The sharp contrast every learner needs is with 대답(對答) 'a (spoken) answer/response': you give a 대답 out loud to a question someone asks face-to-face, but you write a 답장 back to a message. A third neighbor is 회신(回信) 'a reply,' the stiff, formal/business word used in official correspondence. So a casual text-back is 답장, answering a teacher's spoken question is 대답, and a corporate email response is often 회신. Collocations: 답장을 하다/보내다/받다, 답장이 늦다 'reply is late,' 답장이 없다. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'answer/reply' is one word, so learners use 대답 for everything — but if it's written, it's 답장; and bare 답장 isn't a verb, so 'to reply' must be 답장하다 / 답장을 하다. The thing you reply to is marked with 에 (문자에 답장하다).

usage: 외우다 = to memorize by heart; the core study collocation
뜻 = meaning; 단어의 뜻이 뭐예요? 'what does the word mean?'
찾다 = to search/find; 사전에서 단어를 찾다 'look it up in a dictionary'
단어 with the pre-noun 새 'new'; 단어가 새롭다 would put it after
examples: 오늘 새 단어를 배워요.
I learn new words today.
배우다 → 배워요 (요-form); 새 'new' sits right before the noun
이 단어의 뜻이 뭐예요?
What does this word mean?
뜻 'meaning' + 뭐예요? 'what is it?' is the natural way to ask
모르는 단어는 사전에서 찾아요.
I look up words I don't know in a dictionary.
모르는 단어 = words one doesn't know; 사전에서 찾다 = look up in a dictionary
nuance: 단어(單語) is Sino-Korean — 單 'single' + 語 'word/language' — literally 'a single word,' the discrete vocabulary item you study, memorize, and look up. Contrast it with 말 'words/speech/language' in the broad native sense (말이 빠르다 'speaks fast,' 한국말 'Korean'), and with 어휘(語彙) 'vocabulary' as a whole body of words (어휘가 풍부하다 'has a rich vocabulary'). So one item = 단어, the total stock = 어휘, speech in general = 말. The verbs are telling: you 외우다 (memorize) and 찾다 (look up) a 단어, and ask its 뜻 (meaning). Collocations: 새 단어, 단어를 외우다/찾다, 단어 시험 'vocab quiz,' 단어장 'wordbook.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'word' also means 'news/a message' ('send word,' 'have a word'), but those senses are NOT 단어 — 'word from someone' is 소식, and 'have a word/talk' is 이야기/말; 단어 is strictly the linguistic unit you study. Also keep it apart from look-alikes like 단원 'a unit/chapter.'

usage: the quality takes 이/가: 발음이 좋다, NOT 발음을 좋다
연습하다 takes the object 을/를; here you act on 발음
어렵다 is an adjective describing 발음, so again 이/가
to pronounce accurately (lit. pronunciation is exact)
정확하다 = precise/accurate; a common compliment for learners
examples: 발음이 정말 좋아요.
Your pronunciation is really good.
발음이 좋다 with 이 — the pronunciation is the subject being good
이 단어는 발음이 어려워요.
This word is hard to pronounce.
ㅂ-irregular 어렵다 → 어려워요; 발음이 어렵다 keeps 이/가
받침 발음을 매일 연습해요.
I practice the final-consonant sounds every day.
받침 = a syllable-final consonant; 발음을 연습하다 takes 을 because you act on it
nuance: 발음(發音) is Sino-Korean — 發 'to emit/produce' + 音 'sound' — literally 'to produce sound,' i.e. pronunciation, how a word is sounded out. Distinguish it from 억양(抑揚) 'intonation' (the rise and fall of pitch across a sentence) and 발성 'voice production/projection' — 발음 is specifically the articulation of individual sounds and syllables. As a noun it becomes a verb with 하다: 발음하다 'to pronounce.' Collocations: 발음이 좋다/나쁘다/어렵다/정확하다, 발음을 연습하다, 발음 연습 'pronunciation drill,' 받침 발음 'final-consonant pronunciation.' The headline English-speaker pitfall is PARTICLES: 발음 is the SUBJECT of descriptive adjectives, so it's 발음이 좋다/어렵다 (이/가), but the OBJECT of action verbs, so 발음을 연습하다/하다 (을/를). Saying 발음을 좋다 is ungrammatical because 좋다 'to be good' is a stative adjective that can't take a direct object. Also, English 'pronounce' as a verb tempts bare 발음 — you must say 발음하다.

usage: 칭찬 is a noun; 'to praise' = 칭찬하다 / 칭찬을 하다; the person praised takes 을/를
to be praised, to receive praise
받다 (receive) is the natural passive-sense pair: 칭찬을 받다, not 가지다
to get a compliment (lit. hear praise)
듣다 = to hear; praise reaches your ears, so 칭찬을 듣다
to be a sucker for praise (lit. weak to praise)
-에 약하다 = to have a soft spot for; idiomatic
examples: 선생님이 저를 칭찬해 주셨어요.
The teacher praised me.
the praised person takes 를; -아/어 주시다 adds warmth + honors the teacher
칭찬을 들으니까 기분이 좋아요.
Getting a compliment makes me feel good.
-(으)니까 'because'; 칭찬을 듣다 = to hear/receive praise
그 분은 칭찬에 인색해요.
That person is stingy with praise.
칭찬에 인색하다 = sparing with compliments; -에 marks what they're stingy about
nuance: 칭찬(稱讚) is Sino-Korean — 稱 'to call/state' + 讚 'to praise, extol' — literally 'to speak praise,' i.e. to compliment someone's good action or quality. Its clear opposite pair is 비난(非難) 'criticism/blame' (and the everyday 야단/꾸중 'a scolding'), so the axis is praise ↔ blame. Don't confuse 칭찬 with 자랑 'bragging/showing off,' which is praising ONESELF or one's own things, not another person. Collocations: 칭찬을 하다/받다/듣다, 칭찬을 아끼지 않다 'not spare praise,' 칭찬에 인색하다 'stingy with praise,' the proverb 칭찬은 고래도 춤추게 한다 'praise makes even a whale dance.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'give a compliment' tempts 칭찬을 주다, but Korean RECEIVES praise — 칭찬을 받다/듣다 — so 'I got a compliment' is 칭찬을 받았어요/들었어요, never 칭찬을 가졌어요. Also bare 칭찬 isn't a verb; 'to compliment her' is 그녀를 칭찬하다, marking the person with 을/를.

usage: to explain, to give an explanation
설명 is a noun; 'to explain' = 설명하다 / 설명을 하다
-아/어 주세요 frames it as a favor; the polite way to ask for an explanation
자세한 'detailed' before the noun; 설명이 자세하다 puts it after
덧붙이다 = to append/add on; common in writing or talks
examples: 선생님, 설명해 주세요.
Teacher, please explain it.
설명하다 + 주세요 = 'please explain (for me)'; softens the request
한 번 더 설명해 주시겠어요?
Could you explain it one more time?
-아/어 주시겠어요? is extra-polite; 한 번 더 = once more
이 부분은 설명이 좀 부족해요.
This part is a bit short on explanation.
설명이 부족하다 = the explanation is lacking; here 설명 is the subject (이/가)
nuance: 설명(說明) is Sino-Korean — 說 'to tell/speak' + 明 'clear, bright' — literally 'to make clear by telling,' i.e. an explanation of how or why something works. Distinguish it from 설득(說得) 'persuasion' (talking someone INTO agreeing, sharing the 說 root) and from 묘사(描寫) 'description' (depicting what something looks/feels like); 설명 is about clarifying and informing, not convincing or portraying. As a noun it becomes the verb with 하다: 설명하다, very often softened to 설명해 주세요/주시겠어요 'please explain for me.' Collocations: 설명을 하다/듣다, 자세한 설명, 설명이 부족하다/이해가 안 되다, 설명서 'instruction manual.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'explain to me' tempts learners to mark the listener with 를 (저를 설명하다 ✗, which would mean 'explain ME'); the listener takes 한테/에게 (저한테 설명해 주세요), and what you explain takes 을/를. Bare 설명 can't be the verb — use 설명하다. Don't confuse 설명 with the look-alike 설탕 'sugar.'

usage: 전하다 (convey) relays your regards to a third person, often via someone else
to ask after someone (how they're doing)
묻다 (ask) — ㄷ-irregular: 물어요, 물었어요; you inquire about their well-being
안부 + 인사 'greeting'; the set phrase for asking/sending how-are-yous
to a superior, 묻다 becomes humble 여쭙다: 부모님께 안부를 여쭙다
examples: 부모님께 안부 전해 주세요.
Please give my regards to your parents.
께 = honorific 'to'; 전하다 passes your greeting along to them
오랜만에 만나서 서로 안부를 물었어요.
Meeting after a long time, we asked after each other.
서로 = each other; 안부를 묻다 (ㄷ-irregular 물었어요)
선생님께 안부 여쭤 봐 주세요.
Please pass along my regards to the teacher.
여쭙다 = humble 'ask/convey'; used when the person is of higher status
nuance: 안부(安否) is Sino-Korean — 安 'safe, well' + 否 'or not' — literally 'whether (one is) well or not,' i.e. an inquiry into someone's welfare, hence 'regards, well-wishes.' It is not a standalone greeting word like 인사 'a greeting' but the CONTENT of caring after someone, so it lives almost entirely inside two collocations: 안부를 묻다 'ask how someone is' and 안부를 전하다 'send/pass on regards (to a third party).' Contrast 안부 (asking after well-being, often about an absent person) with 인사 (the act/words of greeting someone present) and with 연락 (the channel of contact) — you might 연락해서 안부를 묻다 'get in touch to ask how they are.' Register matters: to elders the verbs go humble — 안부를 여쭙다 (for 묻다) and 안부를 전해 드리다. The English-speaker pitfall: don't attach plain 하다 — there is no natural 안부하다; you must pick 전하다 or 묻다. Also, 안부를 전하다 means relaying regards TO someone else, while asking the person directly is 안부를 묻다 — mixing these reverses who the well-wishing is aimed at.
